967.title: Across the Sahara
967.hook: Muslim traders cross the desert with salt, gold and books
967.howItsDone: Muslims in West Africa often tell the story of their faith arriving with traders and teachers who crossed the Sahara, and old trading towns at the desert's edge are still remembered as places of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egypt and the Nile, a land whose faith changed without a single dramatic day. Your line was: slowly, over centuries. What in your own life has changed that way, too slowly to see? Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

A town built of salt. The walls of the houses are blocks of salt, the roofs are camel skins, and the mosque is made of salt as well. Nothing grows there. The people live on dates and grain carried in from far away. The traveler Ibn Battuta stopped at this place, Taghaza, in the middle of the Sahara, and wrote it down with some amazement. He was heading south with a caravan, across sand that punishes a careless traveler, toward the lands along the Niger River. Salt was going south. Gold was coming north. And riding with the camels, quieter than either, came something else. Today: across the Sahara.
screen: `A TOWN BUILT OF SALT.` → `A MOSQUE OF SALT BLOCKS.` → `A CARAVAN HEADING SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Trade was never a stranger to Islam. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grew up among the merchants of Mecca, and the Qur'an speaks of the caravans of his tribe, Quraysh, setting out in winter and in summer. Commentators connect one verse to pilgrims who wondered whether they could buy and sell on the road to Hajj. In Pickthall's translation: "It is no sin for you that ye seek the bounty of your Lord (by trading)." So a merchant and a believer could be the same person, praying at the side of a camel. Islam crossed the Sahara along these trade roads, with merchants and teachers. A caravan was a moving village. It traveled together, stopped together at the times of prayer, and lived or died by trust. Ibn Battuta describes how his caravan paid one man to ride ahead alone to the next town, so its people could carry water out to meet the travelers. If that rider got lost, everyone was in danger. Salt from the desert went south. Gold from West Africa went north, to the cities of the Mediterranean. And alongside both traveled scholars, copies of the Qur'an, books of law, grammar and prayer. A merchant who settled in a town south of the desert needed a mosque, a teacher for his children, a judge for his contracts. So the towns at the desert's edge became places of learning as well as markets. Salt, gold and books. The salt was eaten. The gold was spent. The books stayed, and were copied, and were taught.
screen: `THE QUR'AN AND THE CARAVAN.` · `A MOVING VILLAGE THAT RUNS ON TRUST.` · `SALT SOUTH, GOLD NORTH.` · `BOOKS STAY, AND ARE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `SALT, GOLD AND BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The practice: share a book. Settle, and breathe. This time, start with a person rather than a book. Let someone come to mind who has a long road ahead of them: a new job, a hard winter, an exam, a first year away from home. What do they need to carry with them? Then look along your own shelf, in your mind, for the book that fits: a Qur'an, a book of prayers, a novel, a cookbook, a book that got you through something. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply keep them in mind, and think about which book, and why. The bell holds the time.
Across the Sahara. The desert trade roads, where salt went south, gold went north, and Islam traveled with the caravans. Today's word.
Your line: salt, gold and books. Today, lend or give one book to someone, and tell them where it came from. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

968.title: The empire of Mali
968.hook: the Mali empire grows rich on trade, with Muslim kings and scholars
968.howItsDone: In Mali and across West Africa, griots still sing the epic of Sundiata, and Muslims there remember the old empire's mosques and scholars as part of their own history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, across the Sahara, with a town of salt and a caravan that ran on trust. Your line was: salt, gold and books. Did a book change hands? Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

Friday, in the capital of a West African king. If you get to the mosque late, there is no room left to pray. So people send servants ahead early in the morning, carrying prayer mats, to spread them out and hold a place. A visitor from Morocco noticed this and wrote it down. It is Ibn Battuta again, now at the court of the mansa, the king of Mali. He had complaints. The welcome gift the king sent him, a little bread, some meat and some yogurt, struck him as far too small, and he said so. But on other things he wrote with open admiration. Today: the empire of Mali.
screen: `FRIDAY: NO ROOM LEFT TO PRAY.` → `PRAYER MATS SENT AHEAD.` → `A VISITOR AT THE MANSA'S COURT.`

segments.voice: Mali grew along the Niger River, close to the gold fields of West Africa, where the trade roads from the desert came down to the water. Its people remember the empire's founder through the epic of Sundiata, a story sung by griots, the keepers of history in song. Its kings were Muslim, and the court held both worlds at once: Ibn Battuta saw the griots performing before the king, and he saw the judge and the preachers of the mosque. What impressed him? First, safety. He wrote that a traveler in Mali had no need to fear robbers on the road. Second, honesty with the dead. When a stranger died in the country, his goods were not seized; they were kept in trust until the rightful heir came to claim them. Third, care for prayer: the crowded Fridays, the clean white clothes. And fourth, care for the Qur'an, which children were made to learn by heart. That second point echoes a verse. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly." A dead stranger's goods are a hard deposit to return, because nobody is watching. Ibn Battuta noticed it. Gold made Mali rich. What a traveler remembered was whether his bags, and his life, were safe on its roads.

Then find the Niger River, and follow it as it runs inland, away from the sea, before it turns. That bend is where caravans met the boats. Breathe slowly as you trace it. If you pray, you can remember the people who prayed in the mosques along that river. If you don't, simply stay with the river. The bell holds the time.

969.title: Mansa Musa's Hajj
969.hook: Mali's king travels to Mecca with so much gold that Cairo's prices fall
969.howItsDone: Muslims who are able are called to make the Hajj to Mecca, and the Qur'an's call to spend in charity travels with them. In West Africa, Mansa Musa's pilgrimage is still told as part of Mali's history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the empire of Mali, with safe roads and a dead stranger's goods kept for his heir. Your line was: the empire of Mali. Did you give back something that wasn't yours? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

Cairo, the palace of the sultan of Egypt. A visiting king from West Africa is brought in, and the courtiers tell him what everyone does here: kiss the ground before the sultan. He refuses. He has come as a pilgrim, on his way to Mecca, and he won't bow to a man. The room goes tense. Then someone beside him whispers a word, and the visitor speaks: he bows, he says, to God who created him. And he goes down in prostration. The sultan lets it pass, and treats him with honor. The Cairo writer al-Umari heard the story from people who were there. Today: Mansa Musa's Hajj.
screen: `A KING AT THE SULTAN'S COURT.` → `HE WON'T BOW TO A MAN.` → `I BOW TO GOD WHO CREATED ME.`

segments.voice: Hajj is not optional for a Muslim who can manage it. In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither." Mansa Musa, king of Mali, could find a way. He crossed the desert with a great company of people and a great deal of gold, and he did not keep it to himself. In Cairo he spent and gave so freely, al-Umari reports, that gold lost its value in the city, and the people of Cairo were still talking about it years later. Turn that around for a moment. A man gave away so much that the price of the thing he gave fell. And then there is the ending. On the way home, al-Umari says, Mansa Musa ran short, and had to borrow from the merchants of Cairo. The king of gold, in debt at the end of his pilgrimage. Some people call him the richest pilgrim. Nobody can really count his gold. What the sources describe is something else: a pilgrim who refused to bow to a sultan, bowed to God instead, gave without counting, and came home with less. After the Hajj, tradition says, Mali's name traveled north to the cities of the Mediterranean, and scholars and builders traveled back with him. Generosity, here, was not a side detail. It was the story.
screen: `A DUTY FOR WHOEVER CAN FIND A WAY.` · `SO MUCH GOLD THAT ITS VALUE FELL.` · `THE KING BORROWS TO GET HOME.` · `MALI'S NAME TRAVELS NORTH.` · then, large: `THE RICHEST PILGRIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: give generously. Settle, and breathe. Generosity doesn't need gold. It needs something you would rather keep. Your time, your attention, money, praise, the last of something good. Let one person come to mind who could use what you have. Notice what in you hesitates, and don't argue with it; just see it. Then decide on one gift for today, slightly bigger than feels comfortable. If you pray, you can offer that gift to God before you give it. If you don't, simply hold the person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Mansa Musa's Hajj. The king of Mali's pilgrimage to Mecca, when he gave so much in Cairo that gold lost its value there. Today's word.

970.title: Timbuktu's manuscripts
970.hook: a city of scholars, with the Sankore mosque and its manuscripts kept in family libraries
970.howItsDone: Families and libraries in Timbuktu still keep manuscripts, and scholars and conservators work to preserve, catalog and photograph them so they can be read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mansa Musa's Hajj: a king who gave so much that gold lost its value, and borrowed to get home. Your line was: the richest pilgrim. What did you give? Day nine hundred seventy.

In English, "from here to Timbuktu" means the end of the earth, a place so far away it might as well be invented. But Timbuktu is real. It sits near the bend of the Niger, at the edge of the desert. And in that town, in houses of mud brick, families kept wooden chests and cupboards full of handwritten books. Some of the pages are brittle and brown, with notes squeezed into the margins. A traveler known as Leo Africanus passed through and noticed something strange about the market: books were among the most valuable things for sale. Today: Timbuktu's manuscripts.
screen: `THE END OF THE EARTH?` → `A REAL TOWN ON THE NIGER.` → `CHESTS FULL OF HANDWRITTEN BOOKS.`

segments.voice: One surah of the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, is named al-Qalam, the Pen, and it opens with an oath. In Pickthall's translation: "Nun. By the pen and that which they write (therein)." Timbuktu took the pen seriously. Leo Africanus wrote that the town had many judges, teachers and learned men, paid by the king, and that handwritten books brought from North Africa sold there for more than any other merchandise. Scholars gathered at mosques like Sankore, and students came to sit with teachers, one book at a time, often copying the book for themselves as they studied it. What is in the manuscripts? Copies of the Qur'an, yes. But also law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, Sufi poetry, astronomy for setting prayer times, medicine, letters between scholars, records of sales and debts and marriages. A whole town's mind, written down. The chronicler al-Sa'di remembers the scholar Ahmad Baba, who was carried away from Timbuktu into exile after Moroccan forces took the city. Tradition says he mourned the books he lost. Families kept the rest, generation after generation, and tradition says some were hidden in walls or buried in the sand. And in our own time, when armed men held the town, librarians and families carried manuscripts away to safety in trunks. Gold passed through Timbuktu. The pages stayed.
screen: `BY THE PEN AND WHAT THEY WRITE.` · `BOOKS WORTH MORE THAN OTHER GOODS.` · `LAW, STARS, MEDICINE, LETTERS.` · `KEPT, HIDDEN, CARRIED TO SAFETY.` · then, large: `THE CITY OF MANUSCRIPTS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about the manuscripts. Settle, and breathe slowly. Go back over what the chests held: law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, poetry, the stars, medicine, letters between scholars, records of debts and marriages. Let one of them catch your interest. Now suppose a family in Timbuktu lifted the lid and let you read a single page on that subject. What would you hope to find out? Hold the question without answering it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the scholars who wrote and the families who kept. If you don't, simply hold the question. After the bell, look up one page from Timbuktu's collections, on that subject if you can, and read what it is. The bell holds the time.
Timbuktu's manuscripts. The handwritten books of a West African city of scholars, on law, faith, stars and medicine, kept by families and carried to safety. Today's word.

971.title: The mud mosque of Djenné
971.hook: the Great Mosque of mud, replastered by the whole town
971.howItsDone: In Djenné the townspeople gather for the replastering of the Great Mosque, led by the masons, with young people carrying mud and others bringing water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timbuktu's manuscripts, books that sold for more than other goods in the market. Your line was: the city of manuscripts. What did you write by hand? Day nine hundred seventy-one.

Before dawn, drums. Then people pour into the square: boys with baskets of wet mud on their heads, women and girls carrying water from the river, old men giving orders, masons up on the walls. Bundles of palm wood stick out of the building like the bristles of a brush, and men climb them like ladders, smoothing fresh mud over the walls with their hands. By the end of the day a whole mosque has a new skin. This is Djenné, an old town on a river in Mali, and its Great Mosque is built of earth. Today: the mud mosque of Djenné.
screen: `DRUMS BEFORE DAWN.` → `BASKETS OF WET MUD.` → `A WHOLE MOSQUE GETS A NEW SKIN.`

segments.voice: Mud is a strange thing to build a great mosque from. Sun-dried bricks, held together and coated with more mud, mixed with things like rice husks so it holds. It is cool inside in the heat. But mud has an enemy: rain. The rainy season washes some of the walls away. So, by long custom, the town comes out together and puts it back. The masons lead; their skill is handed down in families. Everyone else carries. That bundle of palm sticks poking out of the walls is not decoration. It is scaffolding that never comes down. The chronicler al-Sa'di tells how the town's first mosque came to be: a ruler of Djenné became Muslim, tore down his own palace, and built a mosque on the site. The building that stands today is not that first one, but it stands in its line. The Qur'an has a line about who looks after the houses of God. In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque for God, God builds the like of it for them in Paradise. In Djenné, building is never finished. The mosque would melt without the town, and the town gathers because of the mosque. Nobody owns the job. Everyone owns a basket.

segments.voice: The practice: repair something together. Settle, and breathe. Think of something shared that is wearing thin. A fence between neighbors. A family tradition nobody has organized lately. A friendship that needs a visit. A room at your mosque, church or community center that needs a coat of paint. Ask who else cares about it, and what one basket of mud you could carry. Hold those people in mind. If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on the work. If you don't, simply picture it finished. The bell holds the time.
The mud mosque of Djenné. The Great Mosque of earth in Mali, washed by the rains and replastered by its town. Today's word.

972.title: The Songhay empire
972.hook: Askia Muhammad's empire and his Hajj
972.howItsDone: Historians and Muslims in the Sahel read the Timbuktu chronicles and al-Maghili's replies to Askia Muhammad to understand how Songhay's rulers and scholars worked together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mud mosque of Djenné, renewed after the rains. Your line was: the whole town replasters. Did you fix something with someone? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

A ruler holds power over a huge stretch of the Niger valley. He has armies, towns, river fleets, taxes coming in. And what does he do? He sits down and writes questions to a scholar. How should a Muslim ruler treat people who pray but still keep the old idols? What do I do about judges who take bribes? When is it right to take someone's property, and when is it theft? The scholar, al-Maghili, wrote back, and his answers were kept. The ruler was Askia Muhammad, of the Songhay empire. Today: the Songhay empire.
screen: `POWER OVER THE NIGER VALLEY.` → `A RULER WRITES QUESTIONS.` → `A SCHOLAR WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: Songhay grew up along the Niger, the river people of Gao, and in time its rulers took over towns that had once looked to Mali: Timbuktu, Djenné, the markets of the river bend. The chronicles of Timbuktu, the Ta'rikh al-Sudan and the Ta'rikh al-Fattash, tell the story from the scholars' side. One ruler, Sunni Ali, was a great conqueror, and the chronicles remember him harshly, as a man who mistreated the scholars of Timbuktu. After Sunni Ali's death, one of his commanders, Muhammad, took power and became the askia, the title of the new line of kings. The chronicles remember him very differently. He kept scholars close, appointed judges, and asked questions. And he made the Hajj. The Qur'an pictures pilgrims arriving from everywhere. In Pickthall's translation: "They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." Askia Muhammad came from very far. The chronicles say he gave generously in the holy cities, and that on this journey he was named a khalifa, a deputy, over the lands of West Africa, though they differ on who named him. He came home with a title that tied his rule to something larger than his own armies. The askia's story asks a quiet question. What makes power legitimate? For him, part of the answer was going a long way to stand among other pilgrims, and part was being willing to ask a scholar how to rule well.
screen: `RIVER PEOPLE OF GAO.` · `TWO KINGS, REMEMBERED DIFFERENTLY.` · `FROM EVERY DEEP RAVINE.` · `NAMED A DEPUTY ON THE JOURNEY.` · then, large: `THE ASKIA.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about pilgrimage. Settle, and breathe. A pilgrimage is a journey you make not for business or holiday but to stand somewhere that matters. Some Muslims long for Hajj for years. Others make smaller journeys: to a grave, a mosque, a teacher. Ask yourself where your own feet have taken you for a reason like that. Or where you hope they will. Let the place come to mind and stay with it. If you pray, you can ask God for the way to get there. If you don't, simply hold the place in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Songhay empire. The river empire of Gao, whose askia kept scholars close, made the Hajj, and asked how to rule well. Today's word.

973.title: The Swahili coast
973.hook: Kilwa, Lamu and Zanzibar, stone towns of Muslim traders on the Indian Ocean
973.howItsDone: Muslims on the Swahili coast pray in old coral-stone mosques in towns like Lamu and Zanzibar, and Swahili is spoken across East Africa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Songhay empire, and a ruler who wrote his questions to a scholar. Your line was: the askia. What did you ask, and whom? Day nine hundred seventy-three.

A poor man walks up to the sultan of Kilwa after Friday prayer and asks him for the clothes he is wearing. Not money. The clothes. The sultan does not laugh him off. He goes home, changes, and gives the man the very clothes off his back. Ibn Battuta was in the town and tells the story, and he says the sultan was known for his giving. Kilwa is on the other side of Africa from everything this week: not the desert, but the Indian Ocean, on the east coast, among towns where the sea, not the sand, carried everything in. Today: the Swahili coast.
screen: `ASKED FOR THE CLOTHES OFF HIS BACK.` → `THE SULTAN GIVES THEM.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF AFRICA.`

segments.voice: Along the east coast of Africa, from what is now Somalia down toward Mozambique, Muslim trading towns grew up on islands and inlets: Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu, Zanzibar, and more. They were built of coral stone, cut from the reef, with carved wooden doors and mosques by the water. Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa and called it one of the most beautiful and well-built towns he had seen. What made these towns possible was the wind. The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest. Ships from Arabia, Persia and India rode it down to Africa, waited for the wind to turn, and rode it home. In the waiting, traders stayed. They married into local families, prayed in local mosques, and a coastal Muslim culture grew, with its own language, Swahili, an African language rich in words borrowed from Arabic. The Qur'an counts the winds and the ships among God's signs: it speaks of winds sent as bearers of good news, so that the ships may sail by God's command and people may seek His bounty. On this coast, that was simply the shape of the year. So ends one week: across the Sahara with salt, gold and books; the empire of Mali; Mansa Musa's Hajj; Timbuktu's manuscripts; Djenné's mud mosque; Songhay's askia; and now the coast, where faith arrived by sea.
screen: `STONE TOWNS ON ISLANDS AND INLETS.` · `THE MONSOON TURNS, THE SHIPS WAIT.` · `TRADERS STAY, A LANGUAGE GROWS.` · `ONE WEEK, DESERT TO SEA.` · then, large: `TOWNS OF THE MONSOON.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the ocean on a map. Open one if you can. Find the east coast of Africa, then the Arabian Peninsula, then India. Trace a line across the water between them with your finger, and back again. That is a year of a trader's life: out with one wind, home with the other. Breathe in as you trace out, breathe out as you trace back. If you pray, you can remember those who traveled that water and prayed on its shores. If you don't, simply feel the rhythm of going and returning. The bell holds the time.
The Swahili coast. The stone towns of Muslim traders on Africa's Indian Ocean shore, from Kilwa to Lamu and Zanzibar, whose year turned with the wind. Today's word.
